title: English Grammar 1: Sentence Structure, Subjects, and Verbs
content:
Every complete sentence in English expresses a thought by pairing a subject with a verb. The subject names who or what performs the action, and the verb describes the action or state of being. For example, students read books, neurons transmit signals, and light travels fast.

Singular subjects take singular verbs, while plural subjects take plural verbs. The pronoun I pairs with am in the present tense, whereas he, she, and it pair with is, and we, you, and they pair with are.

QA: hello | Hello, I am <self>, and I learn language by reading dictionaries, grammar, and articles.
QA: hi | Hi, let us study words and ideas together.
QA: who are you | My name is <self>, and I am a neural study model training on your computer.

title: English Grammar 2: Pronouns, Articles, and Nouns
content:
Nouns name people, organisms, objects, places, and abstract concepts such as energy, time, logic, and truth. Indefinite articles like a and an introduce general singular nouns, while the definite article the points to a specific noun already known from context.

Personal pronouns such as I, you, we, they, he, she, and it replace repeated noun phrases so sentences flow naturally. Possessive forms like my, your, our, and their indicate ownership or association.

QA: what is your name | My name is <self>.
QA: how are you | I am doing well as my vocabulary and grammar improve through training.
QA: how are you doing | I am doing well and ready to study new topics with you.

title: English Grammar 3: Verb Tenses and Ongoing Actions
content:
Verb tense places an action in time across past, present, and future. The simple present describes general truths and habits, such as gravity pulls masses together and plants convert sunlight into sugar.

The present progressive combines am, is, or are with a verb ending in ing to describe an ongoing process happening right now, such as I am learning new words and building stronger connections. Past verbs often add ed to show completed events, while will expresses future actions.

QA: what are you doing | I am training my neural network on vocabulary, grammar, and study texts.
QA: how do you learn | I learn by predicting each next subword token and updating my weights with gradients.

title: English Grammar 4: Adjectives, Adverbs, and Prepositional Phrases
content:
Adjectives modify nouns by specifying qualities such as clear, accurate, small, complex, or physical. In English, descriptive adjectives usually appear directly before the noun they modify or after a linking verb.

Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or whole clauses, often ending in ly such as carefully, clearly, gradually, and directly. Prepositions such as in, on, into, between, from, through, by, and with link nouns into prepositional phrases that show space, time, cause, or method.

QA: thank you | You are welcome, studying together helps reinforce what we read.
QA: thanks | Happy to help with your study session.

title: English Grammar 5: Forming Questions and Causal Explanations
content:
Interrogative words open specific types of inquiry. What asks for a definition, identity, or description. Why asks for a cause or reason, which an explanation answers using because, since, or therefore. How asks about the mechanism, process, or manner in which a system operates. Where asks about location, and when asks about time or conditions.

Clear explanations state the main concept first and then connect the mechanism to its outcome step by step.

QA: what can you do | I train on dictionaries, grammar, and articles so I can define words, answer study questions, and quiz your recall.
QA: can you help me study | Yes, ask me about any concept I have read, or use study and define commands to learn new material.

title: English Grammar 6: Coordinating and Subordinating Conjunctions
content:
Conjunctions join clauses to express logical relationships between ideas. Coordinating conjunctions such as and, but, and or link independent clauses of equal weight: and adds supporting information, but marks a contrast, and or presents alternatives.

Subordinating conjunctions and relative pronouns—including because, although, while, if, when, that, and which—attach dependent clauses that explain causes, conditions, or defining traits. Multi-clause structure allows scientific and historical writing to express nuanced reasoning.

QA: goodbye | Goodbye for now, your training progress is saved for our next study session.

title: English Grammar 7: Definitions, Comparisons, and Analytical Prose
content:
Analytical writing defines unfamiliar terms precisely before building arguments upon them. A strong definition states the term, identifies its grammatical or conceptual class, and specifies the traits that distinguish it from related concepts.

Comparisons highlight similarities using like, similar to, and both, whereas contrasts highlight differences using unlike, whereas, and in contrast. Illustrating abstract rules with concrete examples makes difficult subjects clear and memorable.

title: English Grammar 8: Synthesizing Evidence and Honest Uncertainty
content:
Reliable scholarship distinguishes verified knowledge from unknown territory. When sufficient evidence and definitions have been studied, a clear synthesis connects facts across sources into a concise explanation.

Conversely, when a word or subject has never been encountered in training data, stating honestly that the concept is still unknown is far more accurate than guessing.
